line: Rappers bandwagon tryna get some likes (21, 21) I do it for the fam’, never for the hype (21, 21)

meaning:
21 Savage is calling out Kodak Black and others who called him out for labeling Nas as irrelevant.

While 21 claimed he means no disrespect, and was saying while he was a legend, he was just not currently relevant, other rappers and media outlets didn’t feel that was the case.

Evidently, Nas moved forward and even recruited 21 for this song, where they both speak on the situation.

line: If Savage like the capo that mean Escobar the don, one mic, one gun

In this bar, 21 pays tribute to Nas' “Nas Escobar” persona from the ‘90s, as well as the man himself.

In mafia hierarchy, a captain or “capo” works under the boss, or “don.” Through this metaphor, 21 acknowledges Nas' seniority to him in the rap game while still giving himself accolades.

line: I got all type of stocks and bonds, Kehinde Wiley on my wall

Here 21 Savage shows his financial schrewdness by citing some of his appreciating assets in place of the more common flexing with luxury goods.

Wiley is known for using the classic techniques of European Old Masters to create uplifting, heroic portraits of Black people. line: They sayin’ that Black music dyin’, I’m sayin’ they wipin’ us out
vault_lines: They sayin’ that Black music dyin’, I'm sayin’ they wipin' us out
meaning:
Hip-hop was created by African Americans during the early 1970s. Over the last three years, arguments concerning the rap genre’s decline have occurred, bringing up several reasons why it was diminishing while mainly concluding that it was only evolving. Here, Nas believes that the genre is fading because of the murder of Black notable artists, which began in 2018 with XXXTENTACION after he was shot in an apparent robbery.

Since then, the genre has lost an artist per year, with many of them dying as a result of gun violence, with artists such as Nipsey Hussle, Pop Smoke, King Von, PnB Rock, Young Dolph, and, most recently, Takeoff, whom Nas was deeply moved by during during the release party for his new album, King’s Disease III.

We’re trying to tell these people out here, man, we’re here for a purpose. We can’t be destroying each other over bullshit. Look at these little brothers and be like don’t shoot; don’t throw your life away. It ain’t worth it. There’s something to live for, something to be here for. All that tough shit is cool when you’re growing up, but we gotta learn that we’re here for a purpose, and there is a design that’s out here to make sure we don’t grow, to make sure that we don’t make it. And we gotta recognize that there is something in existence that’s trying to stop the youth from the hood from growing into its proper purpose.

line: They ain’t know that I see everything, invested in Ring
vault_lines: They ain't know that I see everything, invested in Ring
meaning:
Nas is making a play on the Ring doorbells which have a camera to show the homeowner who is on or around their property even when they’re not home.

He also alludes to foreseeing Ring being successful and acquired by a bigger company, which led him to make an early investment of $4.5 million through his QueensBridge Venture Partners firm in July 2014. Ring was acquired by Amazon for $1.2 billion in 2018, giving Nas a reported return of $40 million.

line: When you turn to legend, no such thing as relevance (21, 21) They must’ve forgot that I’m a new rapper that got integrity (21, 21) All in the media and blogs, that’s just a place I don’t care to be (21, 21) Most of these niggas wouldn’t say shit if they was ahead of me
vault_lines: When you turn to legend, no such thing as relevance (21, 21)
meaning:
During a Clubhouse room on November 13, which was related to the two artists' recent album releases, Drake and 21 Savage’s collaborative album, Her Loss and the final instalment of Nas and Hit-Boy’s series, King’s Disease III, Savage would go on to talk about how the legendary MC is “irrelevant” in current rap, saying:

I don’t feel like he’s relevant […] I just feel like he got a loyal fan base. He still makes good music.

This message caused quite a stir in the rap community and led to several mixed messages about it in social media, with Nas already being recognized as a ‘90s and '00s rap legend. The next day, Savage clarified that people misunderstood it and wanted to give another message that the others took out of context in a tweet, saying:

https://twitter.com/21savage/status/1592272939126493184?s=20&t=GmJmJ8Hgb5E3m3xEYH4qMw

Nas casually responded to the words of the British rapper in an Instagram post the next day with the simple caption:

😂 LOVE

With this song, both artists made each side of the debate disappear, to show the respect that should be shown between old and new Rap artists. Nas would speak in more detail in an Instagram post along with the announcement of the single:

Only way we moving is with love, respect and unity. The foundational principles of hip hop. Excited to collaborate with my young brother and I hope more artist use turbulent moments and turn them into a time to make new art. That’s what it’s about

line: They just ran in one of my cribs and took what? I replaced it (Haha) Two Caucasians, saw part of they faces Most of y’all assumed that they was Black, it’s exploitation (Black Caesar)
vault_lines: They just ran in one of my cribs and took what? I replaced it (Haha)
meaning:
On November 12, 2022, just a day after King’s Disease III was released, it was reported that Nas' Calabasas property was robbed, with burglars getting away with at least two bags' worth of Nas' belongings while he was at his album release party in New York.

However, Nas reveals the burglars were white, and not Black, as some people might have immediately assumed. He faults the media’s long-time negative stereotyping of Black people for the presumption, comparing it to the classic 1973 blaxploitation film Black Caesar.

line: Did my tour with The Wu, I came back and I set the pace (Woah)
vault_lines: Did my tour with The Wu, I came back and I set the pace (Woah)
meaning:
Earlier in 2022, Nas and the Wu-Tang Clan embarked on a joint ‘N.Y. State of Mind’ tour across the US.



A month after the tour concluded, Nas “set the pace” by releasing King’s Disease III, which is not only the most critically acclaimed instalment in the series, but the best-rated hip hop album of 2022.

line: Ain’t no back and forth, ain’t no left or right (21, 21) I got King’s Disease but I move like a knight (21, 21)
vault_lines: Ain't no back and forth, ain’t no left or right (21, 21)
meaning:
21 Savage opens the song with a multifaceted couplet that also shouts out Nas' King’s Disease album trilogy, which includes his latest release, King’s Disease III.

In chess, the king can move one space in any direction, while the knight jumps over other pieces in an “L” shape.



While the king literally moves “back and forth,” this phrase can also refer to an argument or conflict in which combatants trade shots.  While some may have expected such a battle after the hype surrounding 21’s comments about Nas, these lines suggest otherwise.

21 may be further stating that the “king’s disease” (his ego) made him move like a knight in the sense that he “took an L” on this situation.  Or, he may be referring to the unusual, often tricky way the knight moves in the game to highlight the way he’s dodging this potentially losing battle.

Other layers of the line pay respect to Nas' status as an elder of the rap game.  Most obviously, the king outranks those he chooses to grant knighthood.  Furthermore, since Nas has a son named Knight Jones, the line suggests that he is a father figure to rappers like 21, who are following his footsteps.

Nas with his son, Knight Jones.


Finally, these references to monarchical ranks may allude to 21’s British origins.

line: They wanna see me fucked so they could deport me like I’m Shyne
vault_lines: They wanna see me fucked so they could deport me like I'm Shyne
meaning:
Moses Michael Levi Barrow, better known by his stage name Shyne, is a Belizean rapper and writer who was signed to Diddy’s Bad Boy Entertainment in 1998.



Shyne (left) with JAY-Z (center) and Pusha T (right) in 2021.

Following a promising feature run early in his career and directly before the release of his eponymous debut album, Shyne was involved in a nightclub shooting alongside Diddy and then-girlfriend Jennifer Lopez on December 27, 1999 and was subsequently sentenced to ten years in prison for assault. He still released two records, both to substantial commercial success.

Almost nine years into his prison sentence, Shyne was deported back to his home country, Belize, on October 28, 2009. He continued recording music after his deportation, but never reached the same level of popularity as he had at the beginning of his career.

21 Savage was controversially arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers on February 3, 2019, on claims that he was not a United States citizen and was actually a national United Kingdom citizen. While his case remains ongoing, 21 claims that U.S. officials want him to mess up so they have reason to deport him out of the U.S., just like what was done to Shyne 14 years prior.
